extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer (yes or no). The questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and are paired with Wikipedia passages. The dataset contains 16,000 examples split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.publisher: University of Washington; Google AI Language
extraction.citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine using the pipeline from Natural Questions (NQ). Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator for further processing. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were included.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions from NQ are always placed in the train set. The dataset is split into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set. Each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length are selected as likely yes/no questions. Only questions where a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results are kept. Annotators filter questions for being 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page. Questions not answerable from the Wikipedia article are excluded. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used, and each is paired with the selected passage rather than the entire document.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) they decide if the question is 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; (2) for good questions, they find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, or mark it as 'not answerable'; (3) they mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Annotation quality was assessed by having three authors label 110 randomly chosen examples, conferring on disagreements to produce gold-standard labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Due to sufficiently high agreement, singly-annotated examples were used in training/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to produce gold-standard labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated examples used in training/dev/test sets; 3 authors annotated 110 examples for quality assessment)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has been noted to have been updated since the inference analysis was carried out, suggesting ongoing maintenance. The dataset and code are available at https://goo.gl/boolq.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, which has real-world applications in question answering systems. By using naturally occurring questions, the dataset is tied to genuine user information needs rather than artificially constructed scenarios.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: 'Yes' answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The dataset was found to be class imbalanced. Some language patterns in the passage correlate with the answer, as BERT using just the passage reached 66.74% accuracy versus 62.17% majority baseline.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset contains only yes/no questions and may not generalize to other question types. The inference type analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset has been updated since that analysis was carried out. The dataset uses Wikipedia passages, which may not represent all domains. The questions are in English only.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of reading comprehension and natural language inference models. The dataset is intended for yes/no question answering research, testing models' inferential abilities, and transfer learning experiments. It can serve as a benchmark for evaluating models on naturally occurring yes/no questions.
